<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||TRIGONOMETRY|275}}</noinclude>(2) The two sides <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> and the included angle <math>C</math> being given, the angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math> can be determined from the formulae
{{block center|<math>A+B=\pi-C,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>L\tan\tfrac{1}{2}(A-B)=\log(a-b)-\log(a+b)+L\cot\tfrac{1}{2}C,</math>}}
and the side <math>c</math> is then obtained from the formula
{{block center|<math>\log c=\log a+L\sin C-L\sin A.</math>}}

(3) The two sides <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> and the angle <math>A</math> being given, the value of <math>\sin B</math> may be found by means of the formula
{{block center|<math>L\sin B=L\sin A+\log b-\log a;</math>}}
this gives two supplementary values of the angle <math>B</math>, if <math>b\sin A<a</math>. If <math>b\sin A>a</math> there is no solution, and if <math>b\sin A=a</math> there is one solution. In the case <math>b\sin A<a</math>, both values of <math>B</math> give solutions provided <math>b>a</math>, but the acute value only of <math>B</math> is admissible if <math>b<a</math>.

The other side <math>c</math> can be then determined as in case (2).

(4) If two angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math> and a side <math>a</math> are given, the angle <math>C</math> is determined from the formula <math>C=\pi-A-B</math> and the side <math>b</math> from the formula <math>\log b=\log a+L\sin B-L\sin A</math>.

The area of a triangle is half the product of
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Areas of Triangles and Quadrilaterals.}}
a side into the perpendicular from the opposite angle on that side; thus we obtain the expressions <math>\tfrac{1}{2}bc\sin A</math>, <math>\{s(s-a)\ (s-b)(s-c)\}^{\frac{1}{2}}</math> for the area of a triangle. A large collection of formulae for the area of a triangle are given in the ''Annals of Mathematics'' for 1885 by M. Baker.

Let <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, <math>d</math> denote the lengths of the sides <math>AB</math>, <math>BC</math>, <math>CD</math>, <math>DA</math> respectively of any plane quadrilateral and <math>A+C=2\alpha</math>; we may obtain an expression for the area <math>S</math> of the quadrilateral in terms of the sides and the angle <math>\alpha</math>. We have
{{block center|<math>2S=ad\sin A+bc\sin(2\alpha-A)</math>}}
and
{{block center|<math>\tfrac{1}{2}(a^2+d^2-b^2-c^2)=ad\cos A-bc\cos(2\alpha-A);</math>}}
hence <math>4S^2+\tfrac{1}{4}(a^2+d^2-b^2-c^2)^2=a^2d^2+b^2c^2-2abcd\cos 2\alpha</math>. If <math>2s=a+b+c+d</math>, the value of <math>S</math> may be written in the form
{{block center|<math>S=\{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)-abcd\cos^2\alpha\}^{\frac{1}{2}}.</math>}}

Let <math>R</math> denote the radius of the circumscribed circle, <math>r</math> of the inscribed, and <math>r_1</math>, <math>r_2</math>, <math>r_3</math> of the escribed circles of a triangle
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Radii of Circumscribed, Inscribed and Escribed Circles of a Triangle.}}
<math>ABC</math>; the values of these radii are given by the following formulae:—
{{block center|<math>R=abc/4S=a/2\sin A,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>r=S/s=(s-a)\tan\tfrac{1}{2}A=4R\sin\tfrac{1}{2}A\ \sin\tfrac{1}{2}B\ \sin\tfrac{1}{2}C,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>r_1=S/(s-a)=s\ \tan\tfrac{1}{2}A=4R\sin\tfrac{1}{2}A\ \cos\tfrac{1}{2}B\ \cos\tfrac{1}{2}C.</math>}}

{{c|''Spherical Trigonometry.''}}

7. We shall throughout assume such elementary propositions in spherical geometry as are required for the purpose of the investigation of formulae given below.

A spherical triangle is the portion of the surface of a sphere bounded by three arcs of great circles of the sphere. If <math>BC</math>, <math>CA</math>, <math>AB</math> denote these arcs, the circular measure of the
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Definition of Spherical Triangle.}}
angles subtended by these arcs respectively at the centre of the sphere are the sides <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math> of the spherical triangle <math>ABC</math>; and, if the portions of planes passing through these arcs and the centre of the sphere be drawn, the angles between the portions of planes intersecting at <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively are the angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> of the spherical triangle. It is not necessary to consider triangles in which a side is greater than <math>\pi</math>, since we may replace such a side by the remaining arc of the great circle to
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Associated Triangles.}}
which it belongs. Since two great circles intersect each other in two points, there are eight triangles of which the sides are arcs of the same three great circles. If we consider one of these triangles <math>ABC</math> as the fundamental one, then one of the others is equal in all respects to <math>ABC</math>, and the remaining six have each one side equal to, or common with, a side of the triangle <math>ABC</math>, the opposite angle equal to the corresponding angle of <math>ABC</math>, and the other sides and angles supplementary to the corresponding sides and angles of <math>ABC</math>. These triangles may be called the associated triangles of the fundamental one <math>ABC</math>. It follows that from any general formula containing the sides and angles of a spherical triangle we may obtain other formulae by replacing two sides and the two angles opposite to them by their supplements, the remaining side and the remaining angle being unaltered, for such formulae are obtained by applying the given formulae to the associated triangles.

If <math>A'</math>, <math>B'</math>, <math>C'</math> are those poles of the arcs <math>BC</math>, <math>CA</math>, <math>AB</math> respectively which lie upon the same sides of them as the opposite angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, then the triangle <math>A'B'C'</math> is called the polar triangle of the triangle <math>ABC</math>.

[[File:eb1911 v27 p0290 c1f1.png|center|131px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 5.}}

The sides of the polar triangle are <math>\pi-A</math>, <math>\pi-B</math>, <math>\pi-C</math>, and the angles <math>\pi-a</math>, <math>\pi-b</math>, <math>\pi-c</math>. Hence from any general formula connecting the sides and angles of a spherical triangle we may obtain another formula by changing each side into the supplement of the opposite angle and each angle into the supplement of the opposite side.

8. Let <math>O</math> be the centre of the sphere on which is the spherical triangle <math>ABC</math>. Draw <math>AL</math> perpendicular to <math>OC</math> and <math>AM</math> perpendicular to the plane <math>OBC</math>. Then the projection of <math>OA</math> on <math>OB</math> is the sum of the projections of <math>OL</math>, <math>LM</math>, <math>MA</math> on the same straight line. Since <math>AM</math> has no projection on any straight line in the
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Fundamental Equations between Sides and Angles.}}
plane <math>OBC</math>, this gives angles.
{{block center|<math>OA\cos c = OL\cos a + LM\sin a.</math>}}
Now <math>OL = OA\cos b</math>, <math>LM = AL\cos C = OA\sin b\cos C</math>; therefore <math>\cos c = \cos a\cos b + \sin a\sin b\cos C</math>. We may obtain similar formulae by interchanging the letters <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, thus
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\cos a = \cos b\cos c + \sin b\sin c\cos A\\ \cos b = \cos c\cos a + \sin c\sin a\cos B\\ \cos c = \cos a\cos b + \sin a\sin b\cos C\end{array}\right\}</math> (1)}}
These formulae (1) may be regarded as the fundamental equations connecting the sides and angles of a spherical triangle; all the other relations which we shall give below may be deduced analytically from them; we shall, however, in most cases give independent proofs. By using the polar triangle transformation we have the formulae
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\cos A = -\cos B\cos C + \sin B\sin C\cos a\\ \cos B = -\cos C\cos A + \sin C\sin A\cos b\\ \cos C = -\cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B\cos c\end{array}\right\}</math> (2)}}
In the figures we have <math>AM = AL\sin C = r\sin b\sin C</math>, where <math>r</math> denotes the radius of the sphere. By drawing a perpendicular from <math>A</math> on <math>OB</math>, we may in a similar manner show that <math>AM = r\sin c\sin B</math>, therefore
{{block center|<math>\sin B\sin c = \sin C\sin b.</math>}}
By interchanging the sides we have the equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sin A}{\sin a} = \frac{\sin B}{\sin b} = \frac{\sin C}{\sin c} = k</math> (3)}}
we shall find below a symmetrical form for <math>k</math>. If we eliminate <math>\cos b</math> between the first two formulae of (1) we have
{{block center|<math>\cos a\sin^2 c = \sin b\sin c\cos A + \sin c\cos c\sin a\cos B</math>;}}
therefore
{{block center|<math>\cot a\sin c = (\sin b/\sin a)\cos A + \cos c\cos B</math>}}
{{block center|<math>= \sin B\cot A + \cos c\cos B.</math>}}
We thus have the six equations
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\cot a\sin b = \cot A\sin C + \cos b\cos C\\ \cot b\sin a = \cot B\sin C + \cos a\cos C\\ \cot b\sin c = \cot B\sin A + \cos c\cos A\\ \cot c\sin b = \cot C\sin A + \cos b\cos A\\ \cot c\sin a = \cot C\sin B + \cos a\cos B\\ \cot a\sin c = \cot A\sin B + \cos c\cos B\end{array}\right\}</math> (4)}}
When <math>C = \tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math> formula (1) gives
{{block center|<math>\cos c = \cos a\cos b</math> (<math>\alpha</math>)}}
and (3) gives
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\sin b = \sin B\sin c\\ \sin a = \sin A\sin c\end{array}\right\}</math> (<math>\beta</math>)}}
from (4) we get
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\tan a = \tan A\sin b = \tan c\cos B\\ \tan b = \tan B\sin a = \tan c\cos A\end{array}\right\}</math> (<math>\gamma</math>)}}
The formulae
{{block center|<math>\cos c = \cot A\cot B</math> (<math>\epsilon</math>)}}
and
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l}\cos A = \cos A\sin B\\ \cos B = \cos b\sin A\end{array}\right\}</math> (<math>\zeta</math>)}}
follow at once from (<math>\alpha</math>), (<math>\beta</math>), (<math>\gamma</math>). These are the formulae which are used for the solution of right-angled triangles. Napier gave mnemonical rules for remembering them.

The following proposition follows easily from the theorem in equation (3): If <math>AD</math>, <math>BE</math>, <math>CF</math> are three arcs drawn through <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> to meet the opposite sides in <math>D</math>, <math>E</math>, <math>F</math> respectively, and if these arcs pass through a point, the segments of the sides satisfy the relation <math>\sin BD\sin CE\sin AF = \sin CD\sin AE\sin BF</math>; and conversely if this relation is satisfied the arcs pass through a point.

[[File:eb1911 v27 p0290 c2f1.png|center|135px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 6.}}

From this theorem it follows that the three perpendiculars from the angles on the opposite sides, the three bisectors of the angles, and the three arcs from the angles to the middle points of the opposite sides, each pass through a point.

9. If <math>D</math> be the point of intersection of the three
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Formulæ for Sine and Cosine of Half Angles.}}
bisectors of the angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, and if <math>DE</math> be drawn perpendicular to <math>BC</math>, it may be shown that <math>BE = \tfrac{1}{2}(a + c - b)</math> and <math>CE = \tfrac{1}{2}(a + b - c)</math>, and that the angles <math>BDE</math>, <math>ADC</math> are supplementary. We have also <math>\frac{\sin c}{\sin BD} = \frac{\sin ADB}{\sin\frac{1}{2}A}</math>, <math>\frac{\sin b}{\sin CD} = \frac{\sin ADC}{\sin\frac{1}{2}A}</math>; therefore <math>\sin^2\tfrac{1}{2}A = \frac{\sin BD\sin CD\sin CDE\sin BDE}{\sin b\sin c}</math>. But <math>\sin BD\sin BDE = \sin BE = \sin\tfrac{1}{2}(a+c-b)</math>, and <math>\sin CD\sin CDE = \sin CE = \sin\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b-c)</math>; therefore
{{block center|<math>\sin\frac{A}{2} = \left\{\frac{\sin\frac{1}{2}(a+c-b)\sin\frac{1}{2}(a+b-c)}{\sin b\sin c}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}</math> (5)}}
Apply this formula to the associated triangle of which <math>\pi - A</math>, <math>\pi - B</math>, <math>C</math> are the angles and <math>\pi - a</math>, <math>\pi - b</math>, <math>c</math> are the sides; we obtain the formula
{{block center|<math>\cos\frac{A}{2} = \left\{\frac{\sin\frac{1}{2}(b+c-a)\sin\frac{1}{2}(a+b+c)}{\sin b\sin c}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}</math> (6)}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
